title: $ 840 m funding to transform agriculture, create jobs | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:10
-     - {{hitsCtrl.values.hits}}

Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya

IFC Regional Vice President for Asia and the Pacific Sarvesh Suri

The Government in partnership with the World Bank Group and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD), yesterday announced the launch of the Sri Lanka AgriConnect Joint Implementation Plan, a coordinated effort to transform the country’s agrifood sector, create jobs, and strengthen food security.

Aligned with the Government’s national development agenda and Public Investment Programme 2026–2030, as well as the World Bank Group’s Country Partnership Framework, the plan brings together the Government of Sri Lanka, the World Bank Group, IFAD, development partners, financial institutions, agribusinesses, and farmers around a shared vision for a more productive, climate-resilient and market-oriented food sector.

The initiative will help 900,000 farmers gain better access to agricultural value chains by 2030. This will be backed by $550 million in World Bank Group investments and $115 million from IFAD, and help mobilise up to $170 million in private capital over the next five years.

Agriculture and food processing account for at least 15% of Sri Lanka’s GDP, 30% of goods exports and one in three jobs.

Chief Guest at the launch was Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya who reassured that Sri Lanka is committed to transforming agrifood sector from one that primarily produces commodities to one that creates greater value, better jobs and stronger opportunities for rural communities.

“Our farmers, fishers and rural communities are not simply beneficiaries of development, they are partners in building a stronger, more productive and more resilient economy.

The AgriConnect Joint Implementation Plan will directly catalyse Government action under our Public Investment Programme, helping us connect farmers to finance, technology and markets while creating better jobs, attracting private investment and expanding opportunities across rural Sri Lanka,” she said.

IFC Regional Vice President for Asia and the Pacific Sarvesh Suri said:  “Sri Lanka has globally competitive agricultural products and strong entrepreneurial potential.

The priority now is to connect farmers and agribusinesses with the finance, technology and markets they need to scale. By aligning public and private investment – from innovative financing to risk-sharing solutions – AgriConnect can unlock capital, strengthen agribusinesses and create more and better jobs.”

As the first country in South Asia to officially join AgriConnect, Sri Lanka will help build partnerships between farmers and agribusinesses, and advance agriculture finance, digital agriculture and AgTech, alongside cold chains, connectivity, climate-resilient irrigation, skills and research.

The initiative will focus on value chains with strong potential for value addition and exports, including coconut, cinnamon, tea, fisheries, as well as dairy, poultry, aquaculture and horticulture. It will also support greater economic opportunities in lagging regions, including the Northern and Eastern Provinces.

 

AgriConnect will also strengthen coordination among government, development partners and the private sector to tackle policy barriers, address financing constraints and unlock opportunities at scale.

IFAD Associate Vice-President, Department for Country Operations Donal Brown said: “There is a real opportunity to build on the progress already made in Sri Lanka’s rural economy and ensure that investments continue to reach smallholder farmers. Through AgriConnect, we can maintain this momentum and bring together the scale, financing and expertise of all partners to invest in the first mile of food systems. This means translating our shared vision into tangible realities for rural transformation: driving capital into rural areas, generating jobs, and building resilience against future shocks.” 

AgriConnect implementation has already started through the Integrated Rurban Development and Climate Resilience Project (IRDCRP) financed by the International Development Association (IDA), which connects commercially-viable businesses led by smallholder farmers to better financing and more lucrative markets through productive partnerships. IFC, a member of the World Bank Group focused on the private sector, is complementing these efforts by supporting the competitiveness and export potential of Sri Lanka’s cinnamon and coconut industries and expanding access to finance for agribusinesses through direct investments and financial-sector risk-sharing facilities.

title: CCPI inflation rises to 8.3% in Oct. | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:09
-     - 0

Sri Lanka’s Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI)-based headline inflation accelerated to 8.3% year-on-year (YoY) in October from 8% in September, rising above the three-year high recorded in the previous two months and staying above the Central Bank of Sri Lanka’s (CBSL) 5% ±2% target band for a fourth consecutive month.

Headline inflation has risen from 7.3% in July, when it first breached the upper limit of the band, and from 2.1% in October 2025.

In a statement yesterday, the CBSL said food inflation rose marginally to 8.8% in October from 8.7% in September, while non-food inflation increased to 8% from 7.7%.

On a month-on-month basis, the CCPI rose 0.35% in October, up from 0.19% in September. The non-food category contributed 0.33 percentage points, largely owing to higher prices in the restaurants and hotels category, while food contributed a marginal 0.02 percentage points.

Among subcategories, transport inflation rose to 17.6% from 16.3% and restaurants and hotels to 13.4% from 11.5%. Health inflation eased to 2.6% from 4%.

Core inflation, which strips out volatile items such as food and energy, accelerated to 5.6% YoY in October from 5.4% in September and 5.1% in August. Annual average headline inflation rose to 5% from 4.5%.

According to projections made at the September monetary policy round, headline inflation is expected to remain in high single digits through the first quarter of 2027 before easing towards the 5% target, and to remain around the target over the medium term. The CBSL said the projections are conditional on, among other assumptions, the effects of tensions in the Middle East and their spillovers gradually dissipating.

The 5% target, first agreed under the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (MPFA) between the CBSL and the Minister of Finance in October 2023, was retained under a new MPFA signed this month.

title: Heat stress to cost SL $ 26 b, 145,000 jobs a year by 2040: ILO | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:09
-     - 4

Rising workplace heat stress could cost Sri Lanka around $ 26 billion in annual GDP and the equivalent of 145,000 full-time jobs by 2040 even under a low-emissions pathway, the International Labour Organization (ILO) said yesterday, citing new studies on Sri Lanka and the Maldives.

The losses are not only a future risk. Heat stress driven by climate change cost Sri Lanka $ 6.5 billion more in lost output in 2023 than in the average year of the 1985-2014 reference period, and the equivalent of over 120,000 full-time jobs, the ILO said. Agriculture is likely to be the hardest hit, followed by services, manufacturing and construction.

“These findings make clear that heat stress is already affecting workers, enterprises and economies in Sri Lanka and the Maldives. Protecting workers from heat stress needs to be part of how we approach occupational safety and health, climate adaptation and economic resilience. Through social dialogue, governments, employers and workers can develop practical solutions that protect health and livelihoods while sustaining productive enterprises,” ILO Country Director for Sri Lanka and the Maldives Joni Simpson said.

According to the ILO factsheet ‘Impacts of heat stress on jobs and productivity in Sri Lanka’, the services sector accounted for the largest share of the 2023 GDP loss at $ 2.7 billion, or 41.9%, followed by transport and trade at $ 1.25 billion (19.3%). Manufacturing lost $ 920 million (14.1%), agriculture $ 750 million (11.5%), construction $ 655 million (10%) and mining and quarrying $ 211 million (3.2%). The figures are in fixed 2015 prices.

Job losses, proxied from work hours lost, were concentrated in agriculture, which accounted for 48%, or 57,230, of the 120,300 full-time equivalent jobs lost. Services followed with 22% (26,529), manufacturing 13% (15,176), construction 11% (13,154) and transport and trade 6% (7,529).

The economy lost 241 million work hours, or 1.62% of available hours, with agriculture the worst affected at 2.69%. Some 35% of the jobs were lost in the second quarter, the period of most intense heat.

“Reduced labour productivity under high heat stress is not only a matter of slower movement; it also includes reduced work output and increased error rates,” the ILO said.

During the reference period, productivity loss due to heat stress fluctuated between 15% and 18% in agriculture and construction, and held at about 10%-12% in manufacturing, mining and quarrying, services, and transportation and trade.

Sri Lanka’s mean temperature has already risen by about 1°C since the 1960s. Looking ahead, the ILO modelled four Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), the scenarios used by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), ranging from a sustainable, low-emission world (SSP1-2.6) to continued heavy fossil fuel use (SSP5-8.5). Maximum temperature is projected to rise by 2°C under the lower-emission scenarios and by up to 6°C by late century under the highest, while WBGT would rise by about 2°C to as much as 5°C.

Even on the Paris-aligned trajectory (SSP1-2.6), the 2040 loss of $ 26.1 billion, or 11.8% of GDP, would rise to 13%, or $ 65.6 billion, in 2060, relative to baseline losses. Under the middle-of-the-road scenario (SSP2-4.5), the contraction would deepen from 11.5% ($ 21.1 billion) in 2040 to 13.7% ($ 51.7 billion) in 2060. The regional-rivalry scenario (SSP3-7.0) would push the burden to 13.5% by 2060, equal to $ 37.2 billion given the slow economic growth assumed under it. Should fossil-fuel development continue unabated (SSP5-8.5), the loss could reach 15.2%, or $ 87.1 billion, by 2060.

Job losses would follow a similar path. Beyond the 145,000 under SSP1-2.6, the economy would lose the equivalent of 161,000 full-time jobs under SSP2-4.5 and 210,000-220,000 under the high-emission scenarios by 2040. By 2060, losses would range from 158,000, or 2.1% of the labour force, under SSP1-2.6 to over 272,000 under SSP2-4.5, 314,000 under SSP3-7.0 and nearly 349,000 under SSP5-8.5, where heat would cut more than 4.6% of total work hours.

ILO’s recommendations include adjusting working hours to avoid the hottest periods, shade, hydration and cooling stations, heat-tolerant crop varieties, improved ventilation in factories and mines, real-time WBGT monitoring, stronger occupational safety and health standards and greater awareness of heat-related risks. The ILO also stressed the importance of social protection, particularly for workers who cannot reduce their working hours without losing essential income.

title: TIN mandatory for eight transactions from 1 Nov.: IRD reminder | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:08

The Inland Revenue Department (IRD) has reminded the public that a valid Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) certificate will be mandatory for eight specified transactions from 1 November, under the Inland Revenue (Amendment) Act, No. 11 of 2026.

The requirement applies to persons specified under Section 102(3) of the Inland Revenue Act, No. 24 of 2017, as amended. They will need a TIN certificate to open an account at a bank or financial institution, obtain a credit card, obtain approval for a building plan, register a motor vehicle, renew a motor vehicle licence, register land or a land title, register a business, or transfer shares in a Sri Lankan-incorporated company, with the last requiring a certificate from both the transferor and the transferee.

Relevant officials and institutions must ensure the certificate is submitted before processing or completing any of these transactions, the IRD said.

The obligation to obtain a TIN applies to resident individuals aged 18 or above as of 31 December, 2023, and to those who turned or will turn 18 on or after 1 January, 2024, upon reaching that age. It was introduced through Extraordinary Gazette Notification No. 2334/21 of 31 May, 2023.

Individuals without a TIN can register through the IRD’s e-Services portal, where they can also verify their TIN. A printout of the verification result clearly showing the individual’s National Identity Card (NIC) number and TIN may be accepted in place of the official certificate. The Commissioner General of Inland Revenue urged the public to obtain and verify their TIN certificates before the deadline to avoid delays.

title: CMTA calls on Govt. to plug Rs. 120 b revenue leakage linked to 15% depreciation | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:07
-     - 4

From left: David Pieris Motor Company (Lanka) Ltd., Chief Officer (Vehicle Sales) Lakmal De Silva; Kia Motors Lanka Ltd., Chairman Mahen Thambiah; Diesel & Motor Engineering PLC (DIMO) Managing Director Gahanath Pandithage; Ceylon Motor Traders Association (CMTA) Chairman Andrew Perera; Ideal Motors Ltd., Chairman Nalin Welgama; United Motors Lanka PLC Group Chief Operating Officer Charaka Perera; Stafford Motors Ltd., Director Tarindra Kaluperuma; and Associated Motorways Ltd., Group Managing Director Jawahar Ganesh

The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce-affiliated automotive body Ceylon Motor Traders’ Association (CMTA) yesterday urged the Government to take decisive action in the upcoming 2027 Budget to abolish the 15% depreciation concession granted on used vehicle imports.

Doing so, CMTA said, will address significant Government revenue losses and establish a unified tax structure across the automotive sector.

Despite the issue being raised through previous Budget proposals submitted via the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, the necessary policy change remains outstanding. With the upcoming Budget presenting another opportunity to address this long-standing concern, the CMTA stresses that the Government prioritise the matter this time around to safeguard public revenue, eliminate existing market distortions and ensure a fairer, more transparent vehicle taxation system in the country.

The association estimates that Government revenue leakage arising from the current depreciation mechanism amounted to approximately Rs. 40 billion in 2025, rising to an estimated Rs. 120 billion by September 2026. This substantial increase highlights the urgency of addressing the issue, as continued revenue losses place further pressure on public finances at a time when Government revenue is critical to supporting economic recovery, national development and essential public services.

Under the existing system, used vehicles receive a 15% depreciation on their Cost, Insurance and Freight (CIF) value when calculating import duties. However, many vehicles entering Sri Lanka through the used vehicle market are virtually zero-mileage units, with CIF values comparable to those of brand-new vehicles. The CMTA argues that applying a blanket depreciation concession in such circumstances creates an unjustified tax advantage for used vehicle imports, despite the limited difference in the underlying value of the vehicles, while significantly impacting on the revenue collected by the State.

The CMTA maintains that abolishing this concession should form part of a broader effort to establish a unified and equitable tax structure for vehicle imports. A consistent approach to taxation would help eliminate preferential treatment between market segments, reduce opportunities for misuse and create a more transparent and predictable operating environment for importers, consumers and the Government.

The Association also calls on the authorities to strengthen oversight and take decisive action against those exploiting the existing framework for personal gain. Closing loopholes and addressing practices that undermine the intended application of import duties are essential to protecting Government revenue and maintaining the integrity of Sri Lanka’s automotive trade.

While recognising the importance of vehicle affordability, the CMTA emphasises that this objective should not be pursued through selective tax concessions that distort the market and impose a significant cost on the Treasury. If reducing the cost of vehicle ownership is a policy priority, the Association believes that any such measures should be considered within a broader, consistent taxation framework rather than through benefits that favour one category of vehicle imports over another.

The Association further notes that buyers of brand-new vehicles benefit from manufacturer warranties, which can help reduce maintenance and repair expenses during the warranty period. This offers consumers additional assurance regarding reliability, after-sales support and the potential cost of ownership, factors that should also be considered when evaluating policies affecting the new and used vehicle markets.

The CMTA has previously advocated a more structured approach to depreciation, including a framework proposed as far back as 2013 and then continuously proposing same to every Government up to date, under which depreciation would be determined according to vehicle age rather than applied as a flat-rate concession. The proposal envisaged a defined scale with depreciation capped at a maximum of 10% providing a more transparent and equitable basis for calculating vehicle import duties.

While the Association continues to advocate the abolition of the existing 15% concession, it maintains that, should the Government decide to retain a depreciation mechanism, it must be based on a clearly defined and consistently applied framework that reflects vehicle age and is subject to a reasonable cap. Such an approach would help minimise arbitrary tax advantages while improving transparency and protecting State revenue.

As the Government prepares its upcoming budget, the CMTA reiterates that this issue requires urgent attention and can no longer be deferred. Addressing the depreciation concession and establishing a unified vehicle taxation structure would represent an important step towards reducing revenue leakages, strengthening public finances and ensuring a level playing field across Sri Lanka’s automotive sector.

The Association therefore urges the Government to act decisively in the upcoming Budget by abolishing the 15% depreciation concession on used vehicle imports and introducing a fair, transparent and unified taxation framework. With the issue having remained unresolved despite previous representations, the CMTA stresses that the forthcoming budget must provide a clear policy direction and deliver the corrective action needed to protect Government revenue and support a more equitable automotive market.

title: Govt. seeks to reassure unions over labour law reforms | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:05

Labour Deputy Minister Mahinda Jayasinghe

Labour Deputy Minister Mahinda Jayasinghe has sought to reassure trade unions that the proposed labour law reforms are aimed at strengthening workers’ rights rather than weakening existing protections. He said the draft contains several provisions more progressive than existing laws.

Speaking at a consultation on the proposed amendments for the Western Province, held at the Department of Labour auditorium at Mehewara Piyasa, Narahenpita, on Wednesday, Jayasinghe said the Government was prepared to discuss areas requiring further amendment. He asked trade unions to submit any additional proposals or observations in writing before 30 November.

Jayasinghe rejected claims that the reforms were being expedited to meet International Monetary Fund (IMF) requirements, saying the Government was under no obligation to accelerate the process on that basis.

The Government intends to establish a progressive labour law framework suited to the country’s needs and aligned with modern workplace requirements and international labour standards, he said.

Jayasinghe said the process was being conducted transparently with the participation of all stakeholders. An independent 17-member committee appointed to oversee it had held nearly 40 meetings, with no interference in its independence, he said. Trade unions and employers had been given the same draft.

The National Labour Advisory Council (NLAC) had been convened more than 11 times since the present Government took office, and completed sections of the draft were presented to it on 7 August, Jayasinghe said.

The consultation was one of a series of provincial meetings to gather views from the public, trade unions, employers and other stakeholders.

The reforms would consolidate 14 existing labour laws into four Bills covering trade unions, labour relations, occupational safety and termination of employment, the Daily FT reported in October 2025. Labour Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando said in June that a unified labour code was planned by the end of 2026.

Proposals reported in February included flexible working arrangements with shifts of up to 16 hours inclusive of breaks, compulsory overtime in certain situations, a minimum membership of 100 for union recognition, mandatory secret ballots before industrial action, legal status for manpower agencies and contract labour, and relaxed restrictions on night work for women. 

The Free Trade Zones and General Services Employees Union had warned that the proposals could restrict strikes, side-line smaller unions, weaken protection against unfair dismissal, reduce leave entitlements and extend shifts beyond eight hours. The Free Trade Zone Workers’ Collective has called for a worker-centred framework, including retaining the eight-hour day and 40-hour week, union recognition at 25% of eligible workers, longer maternity leave and minimum wages based on a living wage formula.

title: PUCSL says new Electricity Act could unlock power-sector FDI via competition | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:04
-     - 4

PUCSL Director General and CEO Damitha Kumarasinghe

- Pic Ruwan Walpola

By Charumini de Silva

The Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL) believes the new Electricity Act could help attract foreign direct investment (FDI) into the power sector by replacing the traditional single-buyer model with a competitive market that gives investors greater flexibility to sell electricity.

PUCSL Director General and CEO Damitha Kumarasinghe said the Electricity Act No. 36 of 2024, which he said had come into force in March 2026, envisages multiple buyers and suppliers, allowing generators to explore direct supply arrangements with customers rather than relying solely on the national system operator.

“The new Electricity Act gives options for everybody. Options for electricity user and options for investors, both existing and future,” he said at the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026.

Under the previous framework, procurement powers were concentrated within the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB), creating a single-buyer structure.

The new framework envisages a multi-buyer market in which electricity generators could identify buyers and route power to them through the network, subject to the applicable legal and regulatory arrangements.

Kumarasinghe said this could help address procurement-related constraints faced by investors and widen opportunities for private participation in electricity generation and supply.

He stressed, however, that the benefits would depend on completing the outstanding legal steps required to implement the Act fully.

“We need to quickly do the necessary legal actions to create a level playing field,” he said, warning that without these measures, the system could remain overly focused on the national system operator, limiting the benefits for investors and electricity users.

Kumarasinghe said the proposed framework would introduce competition not only for access to the market but also within the market itself. The electricity users could have greater choice over their electricity suppliers, while generators would have more opportunities to compete for customers.

In this environment, the national system operator would need to remain competitive against alternative suppliers, including private generators and electricity users’ own-generation options.

He said PUCSL’s role would be to facilitate investment by ensuring a level playing field and enabling the choices envisaged under the new law.

The regulator’s position complements its call for a simple, transparent and fair wheeling tariff to facilitate electricity transactions between generators and customers using the transmission and distribution network. Kumarasinghe has said such charges should cover network costs and provide a reasonable return without becoming so high that they discourage investment.

A functioning wheeling framework, together with a competitive electricity market, could help energy-intensive businesses secure power supply and give private generators greater certainty over potential buyers. This would be particularly relevant to investors considering data centres and other industries with substantial electricity requirements.

Kumarasinghe said the Government had enacted a forward-looking electricity law and that PUCSL viewed it positively. The priority now, he indicated, was to complete the necessary legal and regulatory work so that investors and electricity uses could benefit from the options it envisages.

The pace and effectiveness of implementation will be critical to determining whether the proposed shift from a single-buyer structure translates into greater competition, more private investment and improved choice for electricity users.

Marking World Thrift Day, celebrated annually on 31 October, Bank of Ceylon (BOC) once again focuses on raising awareness among Sri Lankans about the importance of saving and developing a regular savings habit. 

Established in 1939, the bank celebrates its 87th anniversary in 2026, continuing its longstanding commitment to the financial well-being and economic stability of the people of Sri Lanka while upholding the trust placed in it by generations. Emphasising that saving is essential for building a secure future for individuals as well as the nation, the bank highlights that every rupee saved today is a valuable investment in tomorrow’s financial strength.

 Commenting on the occasion, Senior Deputy General Manager/Head of Development and Branch Banking Badra Kalyanapriya Gurusinghe said: “The financial decisions we make today play a vital role in building a financially secure future. Saving is not something limited to individuals with higher incomes. Anyone can build a secure financial future by regularly saving even a small amount from their income according to their ability. It is particularly important to plan and save from today for children’s futures, education, housing needs and retirement. I invite all Sri Lankans to make saving an integral part of their lifestyles. The Bank of Ceylon remains committed to helping you secure your future through reliable banking services and a range of savings solutions designed to meet your financial needs.”

Accounts such as ‘Ran Kekulu Smart’ and ‘14+’ have been introduced to encourage children to develop the habit of saving from an early age while helping them build a stronger financial future. These accounts offer a range of attractive benefits. The bank also supports children’s educational aspirations by providing incentives such as gifts and scholarships for academic achievements, including success at the Grade Five Scholarship Examination.

 Catering to the diverse financial needs of customers ranging from young adults to senior citizens, the bank offers savings solutions such as ‘BOC 18+’, Flexi Investor and ‘Smart Investor’. These products are designed to complement customers’ lifestyles and future financial goals. In addition, the bank provides special savings facilities for senior citizens, offering the financial support necessary to enjoy retirement with greater security and peace of mind.

title: PAFFREL warns new security, organised crime Bills threaten rights | Daily FT

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

The People’s Action for Free and Fair Elections (PAFFREL) has urged President Anura Kumara Dissanayake to review two proposed laws to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) and tackle organised crime, warning that they could undermine fundamental rights.

In a letter to the President dated yesterday, PAFFREL Executive Director Rohana Hettiarchchi called for a thorough review of the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crime Bill before they are enacted. While welcoming the Government’s commitment to repeal the PTA, he said the Bills contained provisions that could threaten civil liberties, freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and the right to association.

The letter recalled the National People’s Power (NPP) election manifesto pledge to repeal oppressive laws, including the PTA, and guarantee civil rights. It also cited Sri Lanka’s commitments under the European Union’s GSP+ trade concession scheme and United Nations human rights benchmarks set in 2021, stressing that counter-terrorism legislation must comply with international human rights standards.

On the terrorism Bill, PAFFREL said the broad definition of terrorism under Article 3, particularly provisions referring to significant economic harm, could bring peaceful protests, trade union activities and humanitarian assistance within the scope of terrorist offences. It warned that vague terms in Article 8, such as “obstruction” and “interference”, could allow non-terrorist activities to be treated as terrorism, while Article 10’s definition of terrorist publications could restrict calls for peaceful gatherings. Article 15 was criticised for criminalising the failure to provide information without adequately distinguishing intentional withholding from other circumstances.

PAFFREL also raised concerns over expanded enforcement powers. Article 19 would give the armed forces and Coast Guard warrantless arrest powers, removing safeguards that previously required senior police oversight, while Article 26 would allow the Secretary to the Ministry of Defence to issue detention orders of up to one year without effective judicial supervision.

The letter further questioned restrictions on judicial oversight of evidence submitted to the Government Analyst under Article 49, and said Article 39, which gives the Minister power to appoint an independent detention review committee, could compromise the committee’s independence. Under Article 61, the Defence Secretary could declare any location a prohibited place, while senior police officers could obtain court orders restricting individuals’ movements and communications for up to three months.

On the organised crime Bill, PAFFREL warned that relatively minor offences, including intellectual property violations, excise offences and forestry-related breaches, could be classified as serious organised crimes. It also questioned provisions allowing executive detention orders of up to one year, cautioned that the law’s broad scope could be used against trade unions and civil society organisations, and said making confessions to police officers admissible as evidence could undermine the right to a fair trial.

While acknowledging the Government’s responsibility to protect national security and combat terrorism and organised crime, Hettiarchchi urged the President to reconsider both Bills and ensure adequate safeguards against abuse of power. PAFFREL said legislation introduced in the name of national security must not compromise democratic freedoms, fundamental rights or the Government’s commitment to dismantling oppressive laws.

title: Israel’s electoral post-mortem: Caretaker’s paradox and rigid coalition matrix | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:00
-     - 1

The October 2026 election underscores that the era of a monolithic far-right executive branch in Israel has been checked by the electorate, yet the Opposition has failed to construct a seamless alternative.  For the wider Arab world, this signals a transition into an era of highly transactional, defensive, and fractured governance in Jerusalem

The anatomy of a stalemate: Analysing the status quo 

To understand what Benjamin Netanyahu’s political standing means for the Middle East, one must first analyse the internal forces molding his domestic base. Rather than a sudden collapse, the election on 27 October 2026, resulted in a complex political deadlock, cementing Netanyahu’s role as a consummate political survivor while leaving the country facing massive gridlock.

The 7 October reckoning and security failure  

Critics frequently accuse his Government of failing to prevent the assault and subsequent multi-front escalations. They view his strategic maneuvering not only as an effort to prolong regional conflict for personal political survival, but as an affront to the families of the victims who demand accountability. For decades, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s primary contract with the Israeli public was centred on guaranteeing national security. That perception was profoundly challenged during the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.The public has remained deeply divided over the systemic intelligence and operational failures that occurred under his watch. While opponents view his subsequent actions through the lens of political self-preservation, his core supporters continue to view him as the most capable hand to navigate existential multi-front security challenges.

The conscription crisis and domestic fracture  

Netanyahu’s political alliances with ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) parties have increasingly alienated mainstream secular and nationalist voters. The boiling point arrived over military conscription exemptions for Haredi men. While secular Israelis and reservists bore the immense physical and economic burden of ongoing conflicts, Netanyahu’s legislative coordination with ultra-Orthodox parties drawing public ire sparked widespread demands for systemic reform. Opposition figures like Gadi Eisenkot have strongly mobilised voters by campaigning for a “Zionist Government of enlistment” to counter what they characterise as a “draft-dodging bloc.”

Projections of long-term rule: Pros and cons  

As Israel evaluates its long-term direction, the impact of Netanyahu’s historic 19-plus years in office remains a central debate:

Pros: Supporters credit Netanyahu with transforming Israel into a global technological and economic powerhouse, successfully bypassing traditional diplomatic blockades to secure the historic Abraham Accords, and maintaining an unyielding, necessary deterrent posture against Iran and its proxy network.

Cons: Critics point to deepening domestic polarisation, institutional strain caused by controversial judicial overhauls, international isolation over civilian casualties during the regional conflicts, and long-running corruption trials that opponents argue compromise his governance.

The irony of the Kingmakers: The deadlocked results  

Preliminary results from the Israel Central Elections Committee reveals that neither major political bloc secured an outright majority to easily form a Government.

According to official preliminary counts with over 90% of standard ballots processed:

Netanyahu’s Right-Wing Bloc: Projected to hold 53 to 54 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, short of the 61 needed for a majority. Netanyahu’s Likud party remains the largest single party in parliament, outperforming pre-election polling to clinch a projected 26 seats. 

The Opposition “Change” Bloc: Led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot and his Yashar party (projected at 21 seats), the anti-Netanyahu coalition stands at a combined 48 seats. 

The Arab-Led Parties: Spurred by a massive mobilisation rejecting Netanyahu’s platform, Arab-led parties surged to an unprecedented record of 19 seats. 

The Joint List leadership signaled on October 28, that Arab voter turnout had played a decisive role in keeping Netanyahu short of a parliamentary majority. However, because most mainstream Jewish Opposition parties have historically declined to form direct governing coalitions with Arab-led parties, a rigid coalition matrix emerges. Without them, Eisenkot has no clear path to a 61-seat majority, leaving Netanyahu to remain in power as caretaker prime minister indefinitely while political gridlock plays out.

Geopolitical realities for the wider Arab world 

With Netanyahu locked into a caretaker status and neither bloc holding a clear mandate Israel’s strategic posture vis-à-vis its neighbours enters a decisive phase governed by a complex domestic stalemate.

A recalibration of regional conflict 

Netanyahu’s signature regional strategy has been defined by an aggressive, high-stakes confrontation with Iran. The depth of this brinkmanship was laid bare when it emerged that Netanyahu had pressured its Israeli military to authorise pre-election strikes against Tehran; a move that prompted Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to publicly warn security chiefs to resist political exploitation of national defense. While an indefinite caretaker administration technically retains full wartime powers, institutional analysts at the IDI note that transitional Governments are legally bound by a strict “duty of restraint”. Any attempt by Netanyahu to leverage security policy for coalition negotiations will face unprecedented domestic oversight and legal friction from a deeply divided Knesset.

The Abraham accords and Trump’s influence

The normalisation paradigm faces a critical juncture. President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu ahead of the vote and claimed credit on social media for converting what could have been a decisive defeat into a come-from-behind stalemate. Analysts suggest that Trump may use his significant leverage to press Netanyahu into forming a broader unity Government, potentially sidelining far-right extremist ministers like Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. Sidelining far-right elements would remove a primary friction point for Arab capitals like Riyadh, which have conditioned further integration on meaningful diplomatic movement for Palestinians.

Post-War horizons for Palestinian governance

The political gridlock delays a clear post-war roadmap for Gaza and the WB. While Gadi Eisenkot and centrist factions are highly vocal about engaging with international frameworks and U.S.-led peace plans to resolve Gaza’s governance, they lack the parliamentary numbers to bypass Netanyahu. As such, the entry door to comprehensive regional diplomacy remains heavily guarded by a deadlocked domestic system.

Global fallouts of the US-Iran military conflict

The political gridlock in Jerusalem injects profound uncertainty for both Washington and the ME, particularly as a fractured Israeli caretaker Government navigates the fallout of a direct U.S.-Iran military conflict. With Netanyahu lacking a clear majority but retaining full security powers, the U.S. faces an uphill task of managing an unpredictable ally while attempting to contain regional escalation. In a direct confrontation between Washington and Tehran, any unilateral Israeli strike against Iranian assets could instantly drag the U.S. into a deeper, open-ended war, further straining American military and diplomatic resources. For the wider Middle East, this volatile dynamic threatens to destabilise vital maritime trade corridors like the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, triggering severe global economic shocks through spikes in oil prices and disrupted supply chains. As such, Gulf capitals, hemmed in by a gridlocked Israel and an aggressive Iran, find themselves compelled to fast-track localised de-escalation and defensive security pacts, effectively sidelining broader, U.S.-led regional agreements. 

Emerging economic and security scenarios under the stalemate

The ongoing political deadlock, coupled with the fallout of the U.S.-Iran conflict, sets the stage for highly volatile economic and security outcomes. Real-time assessments point toward two primary trajectories:

The Fragmentation Scenario (High Risk): On the security front, an unchecked Israeli caretaker Government operating without a strong legislative mandate might engage in miscalculated tactical escalations against Iranian proxies to assert domestic strength. Economically, this would solidify the closure of vital maritime trade corridors like the Strait of Hormuz. For the global economy, prolonged disruptions there risk driving oil prices past $100 a barrel, severely choking energy-dependent European and Asian markets and inducing a persistent inflationary shock. Within Israel, the lack of a cohesive state budget due to gridlock, paired with astronomical defense spending, threatens to trigger further credit rating downgrades and capital flight.

The Transactional Stabilisation Scenario (Moderate Risk): Alternatively, heavy diplomatic pressure from Washington could force a frozen status quo. In this security framework, Israel shifts toward a purely defensive posture, relying heavily on the US regional air-defense umbrella while avoiding deep offensive incursions. Economically, this baseline stability would allow GCC states to accelerate localised trade corridors and supply-chain workarounds that bypass active conflict zones. While broader regional normalisation agreements would remain frozen, defensive security pacts and energy-sharing agreements between Israel, Jordan, and Egypt would function on a strictly transactional, back-channel basis to protect baseline regional infrastructure.

Broader security dilemmas and implications for the Middle East 

The October 2026 election underscores that the era of a monolithic far-right executive branch in Israel has been checked by the electorate, yet the Opposition has failed to construct a seamless alternative.  For the wider Arab world, this signals a transition into an era of highly transactional, defensive, and fractured governance in Jerusalem. While security concerns across the Israeli political spectrum remain deeply conservative, the immediate future will be dictated by intense coalition bargaining, external pressure from Washington, and the inescapable matrix of a divided parliament.

(The writer is a retired Ambassador and former Foreign Ministry Spokesman. He can be reached at schandrad@hotmail.com)

title: Palihakkara calls for trust-based connectivity and variable geometry in regional cooperation | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:00
-     - 3

Former Foreign Secretary H.M.G.S. Palihakkara

Delivering the inaugural lecture of the SAU-RCSS South Asia Dialogue, Former Foreign Secretary H.M.G.S. Palihakkara has observed that SAARC seems to have gradually but inevitably, ‘normalised’ non-cooperation and they could instead use flexible, variable-geometry arrangements while keeping the wider regional framework open. Contending that this is a best practice of other regions, he called for the removal of the ’unanimity’ requirement which operates like a veto, from the ‘consensus’ rule in SAARC, so that everybody does not have to agree on everything, but can reach common ground on economics, with reservations concerning unbridgeable issues. 

Palihakkara made these observations speaking on the theme ‘Regional Cooperation: Reflections on SAARC and Beyond’, during the South Asia Dialogue - a new joint initiative launched on 23 October 2026, by the Regional Centre for Strategic Studies (RCSS) located in Colombo, Sri Lanka and the South Asian University (SAU), New Delhi, India. Held from the RCSS office with esteemed guests present physically, it connected virtually with SAU students and faculty, RCSS members, alumni and friends spread across the world, and other South Asia watchers. The discussion was chaired by University of Colombo Department of International Relations Professor Chaminda Padmakumara, and the first Sri Lankan PhD awardee from the SAU, who commended the initiation of the South Asia Dialogue.

In opening remarks RCSS Executive Director and Co-Convenor Ambassador Ravinatha Aryasinha noted that the SAU-RCSS Memorandum of Understanding signed on 31 August 2026 and the South Asia Dialogue initiated, were in pursuance of the founding principles of both institutions - to strengthen South Asian identity and to collaborate in independent research, policy debates, and publications, particularly connecting young scholars from SAARC countries. 

The President, South Asian University saw the event as an outcome of the MoU and underlined how spaces for dialogical engagement were the at the core of this partnership, and reaffirmed South Asian University’s mandate to build knowledge across borders. He underlined SAU’s firm commitment to build transformative networks of change across South Asia and saw the SAU-RCSS taking the vision forward. Faculty of International Studies Associate Professor and co-convenor of the series Dr. Shweta Singh, highlighted that the idea of this South Asia Dialogue series was to bring together academics, scholars, practitioners, young people in conversation on the idea of ‘South Asia’ and beyond. She underlined that this is pertinent as we move away from cartographic traps, to think about South Asia as an epistemic category, with its unique history, culture, politics, and ‘lived experience’.  

Elaborating on the theme, Palihakkara pointed out that regional organisations that have been successful such as the ASEAN, not only had different regime and governance styles, but had also not eliminated every territorial and political dispute among its members before launching economic cooperation. However, they developed mechanisms that did not predicate economic cooperation on resolving political disputes. They have thus achieved flourishing cooperation and trade within the region and today command not only economic, but also geopolitical and strategic agency among the giants—China, as well as the West. He observed in this regard that SAARC has much to learn from the ASEAN’s ‘art of the deal’ to depoliticise economics and economise on politics. Trust, in other words, is not sentimental. It is an economic variable.

Palihakkara noting that many express the opinion that SAARC remains hostage to the Pakistan-India adversarial relationship, with Indian diplomatic opinion arguing that Pakistan resistance and cross-border terrorism militate against regional collectivity and integration - which of course deserves to be taken seriously by Pakistan. He also noted that India’s own diplomats have also criticised India’s role in the region as well, where in addition to the asymmetry, India has been ‘too calculative on short term costs and a narrowly conceived approach on regional cooperation. He said, beyond short-term costs, India seems to overlook the long-term strategic advantage of collective prosperity through regional cooperation. 

He contended that small countries Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Maldives also calculate. While there is an opportunity, at the same time dealing with a colossus, brings economic, security, geopolitical implications. So, smaller states while needing access to India’s market, justifiably or otherwise also fear coercive dependence and loss of sovereignty and strategic autonomy for themselves in their public policy choices. Hence India must not expect sovereign assets or strategic loyalty as kickbacks for economic partnership. He observed that thematic considerations will also militate against the successful regional cooperation, as countries will hesitate to invest in regional infrastructure if politics can suddenly destroy the economic calculations - as businesses cannot build reliable supply chains if customs rules can be disrupted because of political differences. Smaller countries will also be cautious if dependence on a dominant neighbour could become unmanageable, hence trust becomes an economic variable and is important. 

During the discussion responding to questions on China’s role within the region and the Belt and Road Initiative, Palihakkara noted that, no small nation in South Asia will play the China card against India, or the India card against China. India too has been recalibrating its relationship with China, expanding investments in partnership with China. He noted that every South Asian country should support India’s rule-based rise, and if democratic India’s ascent is peaceful and rules-based, it is not a threat to be feared but an opportunity to be seized. 

Questions were also raised by students from SAU whether people to people diplomacy can overcome the stalled regionalism of SAARC; how India could build trust among South Asian states via the structural advantages of regionalism without raising concerns regarding asymmetries; and why they are looking to build alternatives to SAARC? Palihakkara noted that if alternative cooperation is pragmatically done, with no geopolitical intentions but based on economic advantage, no country should have an issue. He added, that while trade builds constituencies for stability, connected grids, cross-border supply chains, easier travel, and professional exchanges like what the SAU-RCSS collaboration is doing, makes disruption more costly. That is how it encourages cooperation. Besides ASEAN, the European and African insight goes to show how to achieve advanced regional cooperation, which also makes conflict increasingly irrational for modern state behaviour.

SAU Faculty of International Studies Associate Dean Dr. Dhananjay Tripathi, who delivered the closing remarks, whilst highlighting the importance of people-to-people interaction and the need to build institutions similar to the SAU where people can come together, noted that although history and memory still play a significant role in state interactions, people can still come together where states manage to accommodate. The Vote of Thanks was delivered by RCSS Research/Program Officer Chamika Wijesuriya, who is also a graduate of the SAU.

title: Beyond the killing of Kawanthissa: Political economy and institutional accountability of wildlife conservation | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:00
-     - 5

The death of Kawanthissa is a tragedy we cannot forget. It cannot be dismissed as merely the death of another wild elephant. There are many lessons to be learned from this incident. Above all, it provides an important opportunity to rethink wildlife conservation in Sri Lanka.

Sri Lanka has a long history of protecting wildlife. We have laws, State institutions, and protected areas established for this purpose. Yet, we have still not succeeded sufficiently in protecting the lives of elephants or ensuring the safety of the people, who live alongside them. Why is this the case?

The circumstances that led to Kawanthissa’s death must be established through a proper investigation. If there was a failure to perform official duties, those responsible must be identified. But we must not stop there. We must review the entire system to prevent similar incidents from occurring again.

Wildlife conservation is not merely an environmental issue. It is also connected to the economy, social justice, and governance. Land use, agriculture, tourism, and development projects all affect wildlife. Some groups benefit from these decisions, while others are forced to bear the costs.

In this context, we must ask three simple questions: Who makes the decisions? Who benefits? Who bears the costs?

These three questions are essential to understanding the political economy of wildlife conservation.

Wildlife conservation and the responsibility of State institutions

Sri Lanka has numerous institutions responsible for wildlife conservation. Considerable funds and resources are allocated to them. Yet, the existence of institutions alone is not evidence of success.

How many field visits have officials conducted? How many electric fences have been constructed? How many awareness programmes have been held?

These are important facts. But they are not enough to measure success.

We must ask several other questions. Have human and elephant deaths declined? Has crop damage been reduced? Have elephant habitats been protected? Do injured animals receive prompt treatment?

The success of a state institution should not be measured solely by the amount of work it has carried out. It must be assessed according to the actual results produced by that work.

This requires clear targets, reliable information, and independent evaluations. The officials and institutions responsible must also be clearly identified.

The political economy of human–elephant conflict

Human–elephant conflict is not merely an environmental problem. It directly affects rural economies and 

people’s lives.

For a farmer who regularly suffers elephant damage, the elephant is a threat to income and personal safety. For someone living in a city, however, the elephant may be a symbol of our national heritage.

We must understand both perspectives.

The benefits of wildlife conservation accrue to the entire country. These include tourism revenue, biodiversity, and ecological balance. Yet, the damage caused by wildlife is borne disproportionately by certain rural communities.

This is a problem of the unfair distribution of benefits and costs.

Therefore, wildlife conservation must be linked to the protection of people’s livelihoods. Fair compensation, effective measures to prevent elephant damage, and alternative sources of income are essential.

Protecting elephants and protecting people must not be treated as opposing 

objectives.

Beyond centralised bureaucratic control

Wildlife management requires scientific knowledge. National laws and oversight are also necessary. However, limiting all decisions to a few central institutions can create practical difficulties.

Villagers possess valuable knowledge about elephant routes, elephant behaviour, and areas of risk. Much of this knowledge is based on long-term experience.

Yet, this knowledge is not given sufficient consideration in decision-making.

A district-level conservation programme based on community participation is therefore necessary. Wildlife officials, local authorities, farmer organisations, and researchers should all be involved.

Community participation should not be limited to inviting people to meetings. They must have a genuine opportunity to participate in decisions that affect their lives.

This would make it possible to identify solutions suited to local needs. It would also increase public support for implementing those solutions.

What happened to existing national policies?

Sri Lanka does not need to develop wildlife conservation policies from scratch.

The National Action Plan for Mitigating Human–Elephant Conflict, prepared in 2020, provides an important foundation for this purpose.

The plan recognised that it is not practical to confine elephants exclusively to protected areas. It noted that approximately 70% of the areas inhabited by elephants are also occupied by people.

Therefore, the problem cannot be solved simply by attempting to separate elephants and people completely.

What is needed now is not another policy document. We must determine the extent to which the existing plan has been implemented.

A report is needed on the work completed, programs delayed, and funds spent. The results achieved through those efforts must also be made public.

There is no point in preparing another plan without first identifying why previous plans were not implemented.

(The author is Emeritus Professor of Economics, University of Colombo)

title: Sri Lanka needs to get more value from its trade relationships | Daily FT
summary:
