-     - 3

According to the Sri Lanka Export Development Board, Sri Lankan exports to the UAE reached approximately $341 million in 2025, compared with imports of about $1.44 billion. The UAE was Sri Lanka’s seventh-largest export destination and third-largest source of imports. These figures demonstrate the scale of the relationship, but they do not tell us everything about its economic value

When the United Arab Emirates and Canada signed a new Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement on 27 October, the announcement offered another example of how governments are actively reshaping their international economic relationships. The agreement promises improved market access once implemented, alongside wider cooperation in investment, infrastructure and strategic industries.

For Sri Lanka, the important question is not whether it should pursue an identical agreement. It is whether the country is obtaining sufficient economic value from the trade relationships it already possesses.

That question deserves attention because international trade is not simply a matter of increasing the movement of goods. Countries must also consider how trade contributes to employment, domestic production, foreign exchange earnings and the development of more competitive industries.

The UAE is already an important commercial partner for Sri Lanka.

According to the Sri Lanka Export Development Board, Sri Lankan exports to the UAE reached approximately $341 million in 2025, compared with imports of about $1.44 billion. The UAE was Sri Lanka’s seventh-largest export destination and third-largest source of imports.

These figures demonstrate the scale of the relationship, but they do not tell us everything about its economic value.

A bilateral merchandise trade imbalance should not automatically be treated as evidence of an unhealthy relationship. Imports can support domestic production, transportation, energy supply and other essential economic activities. Their contribution depends on what is purchased and how effectively those inputs are used.

Nevertheless, the figures provide a reason to examine whether Sri Lankan companies could generate greater value from their existing access to Gulf markets.

Among Sri Lanka’s principal exports to the UAE in 2025 were tea, garments, diamonds, cocoa preparations, coconut products and petroleum oils.

The diversity of these products presents different commercial possibilities.

For tea exporters, the challenge is not necessarily finding another destination for an established product. It may involve developing stronger brands, improving packaging, identifying higher-value customer segments and building relationships with distributors who understand regional demand.

For apparel manufacturers, competitiveness increasingly depends on reliability, design, production standards and the ability to respond to changing customer requirements.

For coconut-based food producers, opportunities may involve product differentiation, quality assurance and consistent access to retail and food-service markets.

None of these possibilities is guaranteed. Each requires careful market research, regulatory compliance and commercial execution.

In my view, a useful trade strategy should distinguish between exporting more and earning more value from exports.

A company that sells larger volumes at weak margins may become more exposed to transport costs, currency movements and financing pressures. A smaller exporter that develops a recognised product and stable distribution arrangements may create greater long-term value.

This is particularly relevant for small and medium-sized enterprises that cannot easily absorb the costs of unsuccessful overseas expansion.

The UAE’s position as an international commercial and logistics centre creates potential access to customers beyond its domestic market. But such access should not be confused with automatic market entry into other countries.

Distribution arrangements, customs rules, product standards and destination-market requirements still matter. Businesses should examine the full commercial chain rather than assume that shipping goods through an international hub provides unrestricted access elsewhere.

The recent UAE-Canada agreement illustrates how trade cooperation can develop alongside investment and infrastructure planning.

Canadian and Emirati institutions have announced initiatives involving energy and international logistics. A memorandum concerning the Port of Churchill, the Hudson Bay Railway and DP World’s international network is intended to explore new transportation opportunities.

The proposal is not yet an operational corridor. Its significance lies in the attention being given to connectivity and alternative commercial routes.

Sri Lankan policymakers and businesses should consider a related issue: how dependable are the systems connecting domestic producers to foreign customers?

A tea exporter may secure an attractive contract but lose competitiveness through inconsistent delivery. A garment manufacturer may invest in production capacity yet remain vulnerable to delays affecting imported materials. A food producer may meet customer expectations but encounter difficulties with documentation or distribution.

Such problems cannot always be solved by signing additional trade agreements.

They require improvements in operational coordination, logistics reliability, standards compliance, digital processes and commercial information.

Export-support institutions can help by connecting companies to buyers, providing accurate market intelligence and improving knowledge of regulatory requirements. Financial institutions can contribute by offering suitable trade-finance products, subject to responsible risk assessment.

Meanwhile, businesses must examine their own exposure to concentrated customers, suppliers and transportation arrangements.

The objective should not be to eliminate commercial risk, which is impossible. It should be to ensure that expansion does not create dependencies that management cannot understand or control.

There is also value in considering service exports alongside physical goods.

Sri Lanka possesses professional skills and business capabilities that may have applications in technology, engineering support, business services and specialised operations. These opportunities depend on market demand, contractual requirements and the ability to deliver services consistently across borders.

International competitiveness should be developed through capabilities that companies can demonstrate, not through optimistic assumptions about future demand.

For Sri Lanka, the UAE relationship offers an existing platform from which to examine these issues. Its commercial importance is already established. The question is how businesses can make that relationship more productive.

The agreement between Canada and the UAE provides a reminder that economic partnerships are changing as countries seek new markets and strengthen commercial connections.

Sri Lanka does not need to copy every agreement announced elsewhere. It needs to understand which weaknesses limit the value of its present relationships and which improvements would allow local businesses to compete more effectively.

The future of trade should not be measured only by how many products cross a border.

It should also be measured by how much sustainable economic value remains with the people and businesses producing them.

(The author is a UAE-based author and independent researcher specialising in security, risk management, operational resilience and institutional governance)

title: Sri Lanka could turn Maldives’ dollar dilemma into investment opportunity | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:00
-     - 2

As the Maldives tightens its grip on tourism dollars, Sri Lanka has an opportunity to position itself as the preferred destination for the next generation of resort investments, international hotel brands and hospitality capital

There is a revealing incongruity at the heart of the Maldives’ latest foreign-exchange policy. A country whose economic model depends overwhelmingly on attracting foreign visitors and earning hard currency is tightening its grip on the dollars generated by its tourism industry. The decision to require Category A tourism establishments to convert 40 per cent of their monthly gross foreign-currency sales, effective from September 2026, comes amid renewed pressure on the country’s foreign-exchange position.

The Maldives Monetary Authority’s August figures showed official reserve assets rising marginally to $ 643.8 million, while usable reserves fell 9.6 per cent to $ 200.6 million. The central bank attributed the decline to foreign-currency sales exceeding inflows during the month.

The timing matters. This is not an isolated regulatory adjustment but a broader attempt to draw tourism earnings into the formal banking system, strengthen domestic foreign-exchange liquidity and reduce pressure on the currency market. President Mohamed Muizzu ratified the First Amendment to the Foreign Currency Act on 31 August, with the amendments taking effect on 1 September. Category A establishments must now convert 40 per cent of monthly gross foreign-currency sales through an MMA-licensed bank, replacing the previous option of converting $500 per tourist.

But the consequences extend beyond monetary management. They raise a question for the Indian Ocean tourism market, what happens when a government requires the businesses generating foreign currency to surrender a larger share of their earnings, while those same businesses depend on dollars to operate?

For Sri Lanka, the answer could influence the next generation of resort developments, international hotel partnerships and investment decisions.

A tighter grip on tourism dollars

The amended framework compresses the conversion timetable. September earnings must be converted by 28 October, rather than by the 28th day of the third subsequent month under the previous arrangement. Compliance records and transaction logs must be submitted through the MMA’s Foreign Exchange Portal.

The authorities have also strengthened controls over foreign-exchange transactions. The revised regime provides for penalties of up to MVR 1 million for prohibited foreign-currency transactions conducted above rates authorised by the central bank. It also introduces restrictions on publishing or disseminating unofficial exchange rates, including through media and digital channels, alongside stricter licensing requirements for money changers.

Money-exchange operators must obtain formal MMA licences and meet a mandatory $50,000 security-deposit requirement. Together, these measures seek to reduce unregulated currency dealing and direct more foreign-exchange transactions through authorised institutions.

The underlying objective is understandable. When dollars earned from tourism do not circulate adequately through the formal financial system, the central bank has fewer resources to meet import requirements and ease shortages. However, enforcement alone cannot resolve the economic incentives that drive businesses towards alternative channels.

The dollar paradox facing resorts

A Maldivian resort is an unusually foreign-currency-intensive business. Imported food and beverages, fuel, equipment, insurance, spare parts, overseas services and foreign-currency financing account for substantial operating requirements.

The resort earns dollars from international visitors but also needs those dollars to remain commercially viable.

The difficulty emerges when mandatory conversion into Rufiyaa is not matched by reliable access to foreign currency for legitimate international payments. Businesses may receive local currency through conversion only to face delays, additional costs or uncertainty when purchasing dollars to pay overseas suppliers, service foreign debt or settle foreign-currency obligations.

At a 40 per cent conversion threshold, this becomes a material consideration for working capital, margins and investment returns.

The regulatory framework recognises that a uniform requirement may create difficulties for certain operators. The MMA Governor has discretionary powers to reduce the threshold where businesses demonstrate that compliance would impair their ability to service foreign debt, pay mandatory foreign-currency taxes or meet essential overseas operating costs.

Such concessions may provide relief, but discretionary exemptions are not necessarily equivalent to a predictable, transparent system guaranteeing access to foreign currency when legitimate commercial obligations fall due.

Taxing offshore tourism transactions

The foreign-exchange measures also intersect with efforts to capture more value from tourism transactions arranged outside the Maldives.

Revisions to the Tourism Goods and Services Tax framework target foreign tour operators and online travel agencies, bringing offshore package and booking arrangements within a more clearly defined domestic tax-compliance regime.

Resorts and guesthouses are required to disclose transactions, booking values and revenue arrangements involving foreign travel intermediaries to the Maldives Inland Revenue Authority.

The policy challenge is to ensure that tourism-related economic activity is appropriately reported and taxed, even when booking and payment arrangements cross national borders. Yet taxation, foreign-exchange conversion and access to dollars are distinct issues. Their combined effect on resort cash flow and investment returns will matter to operators assessing future projects.

Commercial banks also face foreign-currency surrender obligations requiring them to transfer prescribed portions of foreign currency purchased to the MMA. The objective is to strengthen central-bank reserves and support essential imports, including fuel, food and pharmaceuticals.

The wider question is whether the system can improve the availability of dollars across the economy without undermining the businesses responsible for generating them.

Why Sri Lanka should look beyond tourist arrivals

This is where the story becomes particularly relevant for Sri Lanka.

Sri Lanka has experienced its own severe foreign-exchange crisis and has no reason to assume that its present position is permanently secure. Nevertheless, the country has an opportunity to compete for international tourism capital by offering investors a credible, predictable operating environment.

An investor evaluating an Indian Ocean resort does not compare beaches, room rates and tourist arrivals alone. The calculation includes financing costs, foreign-currency liquidity, imported operating expenses, debt servicing, taxation, regulatory predictability and the ability to repatriate legitimate returns.

The distinction is important. A tourist may change destinations for a week. An international hotel group may commit hundreds of millions of dollars to a project expected to operate for decades.

Sri Lanka should therefore resist treating the Maldives’ regulatory changes merely as an opportunity to attract displaced visitors. The larger prize is investment capital: new resorts, hotel-management agreements, integrated tourism developments and long-term hospitality infrastructure.

Colombo should engage international hotel groups and resort operators while investment decisions are still being made. Its proposition should combine a diversified tourism offering, connectivity, luxury and experiential tourism opportunities, infrastructure development and a transparent framework for managing foreign-currency earnings.

The objective should not be to promise investors that Sri Lanka will never experience currency pressure. It should be to demonstrate that legitimate foreign-currency obligations can be managed through predictable rules and functioning financial markets.

A window, not a guaranteed windfall

The opportunity is neither automatic nor permanent.

The Maldivian government could modify the 40 per cent threshold, expand exemptions or improve access to dollars through domestic banks. Its established luxury-tourism brand, existing resort infrastructure and international commercial relationships remain formidable advantages. A regulatory change does not mean international investors will abandon existing projects.

The more important question is what happens at the margin: where the next resort is built, where the next hotel-management agreement is signed and where international capital is committed.

For Sri Lanka, converting this opening into investment requires credible policy, efficient approvals, reliable infrastructure, regulatory stability and a clear commitment to protecting the commercial viability of tourism projects. Without these, any advantage created by developments elsewhere will remain theoretical.

Maldives’ foreign-exchange difficulties should not be celebrated. They should be studied.

The Maldives may have a foreign-exchange problem. Sri Lanka has an investment problem. One country is attempting to retain more of the dollars generated by tourism; the other needs to attract more foreign capital into its tourism economy.

If Colombo can align its tourism, investment, foreign-exchange and infrastructure policies intelligently, the Maldivian policy shift could create an opening that extends far beyond the next tourist arrival.

The question is whether Sri Lanka will recognise that opportunity while it is still a window, rather than discovering it after the capital has already chosen where to go.

(The author is a consultant specialising in data analytics, with a special focus on Sri Lanka’s future direction, sustainable energy, ESG, investments and telecommunications. He can be reached at jithendra.antonio@gmail.com.)

title: Tourism development for dummies? Not quite | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:00
-     - 1

This article explains in simple terms why tourism development is a complex task, far more challenging than many of the seemingly straightforward solutions being suggested today. It looks at the bigger picture and why successful tourism development requires much more than attracting more tourists, targeting high spenders or launching promotional campaigns

There is much discussion these days about the future direction of Sri Lanka tourism. Almost everyone seems to have an opinion about what should be done. Some say we must attract more tourists. Others insist that we should forget about numbers and concentrate only on high-value tourists who spend more money. There are calls for better marketing, more international airlines, new hotels, better infrastructure and a host of other initiatives.

With the widespread use of social media and the emergence of AI tools such as ChatGPT, there is certainly no shortage of advice and recommendations. Some of these suggestions are quite sensible, while others seem to be made without a proper understanding of how the tourism industry really works.

We cannot all be high value

One of the most frequently heard suggestions is that Sri Lanka must move towards high-value tourism. Certainly, we must earn more from tourism. But does that mean we should concentrate only on wealthy visitors?

There is a misconception that high-value tourism simply means attracting rich tourists who stay in expensive luxury hotels. While this segment is certainly important, it is only one part of the tourism market.

Tourists come from different backgrounds, with different interests, expectations and spending capacities. There are backpackers, young independent travellers, families, middle-income holidaymakers, nature lovers, adventure seekers, cultural tourists, wellness travellers and affluent visitors seeking exclusive experiences.

In fact, the middle segment is perhaps the most important of all. It provides a reasonably stable flow of visitors, supports a wide range of hotels and tourism businesses, and helps sustain employment across the industry.

The lower-spending segment also has a role. A backpacker may not spend much on accommodation, but may stay longer, eat at small local restaurants, use public transport and spend money in villages and communities that may otherwise receive little benefit from tourism.

What we need is a healthy and carefully managed mix of visitors, with a gradual improvement in the overall value that tourism brings to the country.

This is the basic thinking behind the Managed Yield, Controlled Volume and Diversified Tourism (MYCVD) model that I have been advocating. (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/new-tourism-strategy-model-balanced-sri-lanka-srilal-miththapala-pzsic/) 

Changing the market mix is not like turning on a tap

We cannot simply announce that from next year we want more high-value tourists and expect them to arrive.

These visitors have different expectations. They may want better accommodation, comfortable and reliable transport, good restaurants, interesting experiences, knowledgeable guides, efficient airports, clean public facilities and professional service.

Tourism is a discretionary purchase. Nobody has to come to Sri Lanka for a holiday. There are many other attractive destinations competing for the same traveller.

Therefore, before we start promising a better tourism experience, we must first make sure that we can deliver it.

This is where I have concerns of arbitrarily setting tourism targets. The latest is that by 2030 we are planning to reach 4 million arrivals and earn $ 10 billion.Which means in four years we hope to double our arrivals and triple our earnings, and we still don’t have a strategy and marketing plan to do so yet. From what I know no Asian country had managed to do this in the past. 

Everything is connected

Suppose we want to develop the Eastern Province as a more attractive destination for middle- and higher-spending tourists.

First, tourists must be able to reach the area conveniently. This means good roads, reliable transport, perhaps improved domestic air services, and better connections with other important destinations.

We also need interesting things for visitors to do. Simply staying in a hotel and going to the beach will not be sufficient for many travellers. There must be properly developed excursions, nature experiences, cultural activities, marine recreation, local food experiences and opportunities to engage with communities.

We need reliable electricity, water supplies, waste management, public conveniences, safety arrangements and effective local administration.

Then, having developed a worthwhile product, we must identify which international markets are most likely to be interested, and undertake carefully targeted marketing and promotional campaigns.

All this takes planning, money, trained people, coordination and, most importantly, time.

There is little point in promoting a destination internationally if tourists cannot reach it conveniently. There is little point in building new hotels if there are insufficient trained employees to operate them, and attracting more visitors to an already crowded attraction without first improving its management.

Unfortunately, tourism development is sometimes approached as a collection of separate projects rather than as one coordinated program.

We have attractions. But are we managing them properly?

Sri Lanka is blessed  to have an extraordinary concentration of natural and cultural attractions within a relatively small area.

At certain times, visitors to attractions such as Sigiriya and Yala encounter overcrowding, long queues, traffic congestion and poor visitor management.

The solution is not necessarily to stop visitors coming. It is to manage the attractions better, regulate visitor flows where necessary, improve facilities, introduce appropriate technology, and develop alternative attractions and experiences that can spread visitors more widely.

There are many lesser-known places in Sri Lanka that have considerable tourism potential. But they cannot simply be opened up indiscriminately. They must be carefully developed with proper environmental safeguards, visitor facilities, trained personnel and management systems.

This is particularly important in wildlife and nature tourism, where the very attraction that draws visitors can be damaged by excessive or poorly managed visitation.

The people problem

Who is going to look after all these tourists?

Sri Lanka’s tourism industry has experienced a serious loss of trained and experienced personnel over the past several years. Many skilled employees have left the country, while others have moved into different occupations.

We need better practical training, language skills, customer service, supervisory capabilities, professional guiding, culinary skills and management development.

We also need to make tourism employment more attractive by improving working conditions, career opportunities and the recognition given to skilled employees.

And developing people takes time. We cannot produce an experienced chef, a good hotel manager or a knowledgeable wildlife guide overnight.

More revenue. But who benefits?

We often discuss tourism earnings in billions of dollars, but rarely examine how widely these earnings are distributed through the economy.

A tourist staying at an expensive hotel may contribute substantial revenue to the establishment. But how much of that spending reaches local farmers, fishermen, transport operators, small restaurants, guides, craft producers and other businesses?

If we are serious about making tourism a driver of national economic development, we must deliberately create stronger links between tourism businesses and surrounding communities.

It means creating genuine opportunities for local people to supply goods and services, develop small businesses, participate in tourism experiences and earn a reasonable income from the industry.

A higher-value tourism industry should not simply mean more profitable hotels. It should mean greater economic value reaching a wider section of society.

This is why diversification is such an important part of the MYCVD approach. We need to spread tourism geographically, across different products and experiences, and across a wider range of businesses and communities.

Marketing cannot work in isolation

We must first decide which visitor segments we want to attract, understand their needs and expectations, and develop the products and services that will appeal to them.

For example, promoting wildlife photography holidays, wellness retreats, cultural experiences or premium nature tourism requires quite different approaches from promoting conventional beach holidays.

There is no point in spending millions telling the world what a wonderful destination Sri Lanka is if the product we offer does not consistently live up to that promise.

In tourism, as in any other business, we must be careful not to over-promise and under-deliver.

Positioning and branding – What does Sri Lanka really stand for?

Another important issue that we seem to be still groping around in the dark about is Sri Lanka’s positioning as a tourism destination. What exactly is our unique selling proposition (USP)? What makes us different from the many other destinations competing for the same tourists? We have beautiful beaches, wildlife, culture, heritage and nature, but so do many other countries. Simply saying that we have everything in one small island is not enough. 

We need to clearly identify what makes the Sri Lankan experience truly distinctive, decide which markets and visitor segments we want to appeal to, and develop a strong, consistent destination brand around that promise. And importantly, the actual experience we offer must live up to that promise. Without such clear positioning, our marketing campaigns risk becoming a collection of attractive pictures and catchy slogans, without a strong message that sets Sri Lanka apart.

A gradual transition, not an overnight miracle

In the MYCVD model, i have considered a gradual transition from approximately 2.7 million arrivals in 2026 towards a planning threshold of around 4.5 million by 2032. Rather than assuming that all these visitors will be high-spending tourists, the model envisages a more balanced market, with approximately 35% in the lower-spending segment, 45% in the middle segment and 20% in the higher-spending segment by 2032.

Based on different assumptions about how successfully the industry develops, we have considered three possible tourism earnings outcomes for 2032: a conservative scenario of US$6.5 billion, a central MYCVD target of US$7.5 billion, and a more ambitious stretch scenario of US$8 billion.

It requires improvements in the entire tourism offering, a gradual shift in the visitor mix, better connectivity, stronger service standards, more attractive experiences and greater spending opportunities.

And there is another important consideration. We cannot keep increasing visitor numbers indefinitely. The carrying-capacity research that my colleague and I undertook earlier (https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/tourist-arrivals-how-much-enough-srilal-miththapala-dafuc/) suggested a broad national planning threshold of around 4.2–4.5 million annual visitors.

This is not a rigid scientific ceiling for every part of the country, but it is a useful warning that growth must be managed with due regard to infrastructure, environmental limits and the quality of the visitor experience.

Who is looking after the bigger picture?

Airports, aviation, railways, roads, wildlife conservation, archaeology, local government, environmental protection, vocational training, investment promotion and many other areas all play an important role. So proper tourism development actually cuts across many ministries. 

But tourists do not experience Sri Lanka as a collection of government departments. They experience it as one destination.

A tourist does not care whether a badly maintained access road is the responsibility of the Road Development Authority or a local council. Nor does a visitor distinguish between the different agencies responsible for poor facilities at a national park or archaeological site.

That is why tourism needs a properly coordinated national development strategy, with clear priorities, responsibilities, budgets, timelines and mechanisms to monitor implementation.

But preparing a plan is only the beginning. The real test is whether the necessary agencies work together to implement it, whether funding is available, and whether someone is held responsible for delivering the results.

Seeing the whole picture

We cannot develop airports without considering transport connections, build new hotels without developing skilled people, attract higher-spending visitors without offering experiences that justify their expenditure, and cannot claim tourism is benefiting the country unless a reasonable share of those benefits reaches ordinary people.

Are we developing the entire tourism industry in a coordinated manner to attract the right mix of visitors, give them a worthwhile experience, earn more from their visits, and distribute those benefits more widely, without damaging the very assets that attract them?

And unless we begin to see it, we may continue celebrating impressive arrival numbers and announcing ambitious revenue targets, without making the fundamental changes needed to build a genuinely successful and sustainable tourism industry.

title: ‘Saving a Tomorrow’: National responsibility beyond saving money | Daily FT
summary:
Saturday, 31 October 2026 00:00
-     - 2

Saving for the future is one of the most valuable financial and social habits that individuals can cultivate. It is not merely a matter of managing money; rather, it is a fundamental principle that determines the financial security of individuals, the stability of families, the resilience of communities and the long-term economic prosperity of a nation. However, in the face of the economic, social and environmental challenges confronting the world today, the time has come to broaden our traditional understanding of thrift and redefine its relevance to the contemporary society.

Traditionally, thrift has been understood as the practice of setting aside a portion of one’s earnings to meet future needs. While this principle remains as important as ever, we now live in a world where financial security alone cannot guarantee a safe and prosperous future. A future without clean water, a healthy environment, adequate food, sustainable energy, natural resources and biodiversity cannot be considered secure, regardless of the financial wealth we may accumulate.

Therefore, the most important question we must ask ourselves today is not simply how much money we are saving for our children, but how much of the world we are preserving for them to inherit. It is with this broader understanding of our responsibility towards future generations that the National Savings Bank has selected “Saving a Tomorrow” as the national theme for the Thrift Month 2026.

Our intention is to extend the meaning of thrift beyond financial savings to encompass environmental conservation, the responsible utilisation of natural resources, energy efficiency, sustainable consumption and the preservation of our national heritage. More importantly, we seek to establish thrift as a shared national responsibility that requires the active participation of every individual, institution and community.

Thrift and future of the national economy

Domestic savings play a fundamental role in strengthening the economic stability and long-term development of a nation. Savings accumulated by individuals and households become an important source of financial resources that can be channeled through the banking system towards national investment, entrepreneurship, housing development and other productive economic activities.

When an individual develops the habit of saving, it strengthens personal financial security. When that habit becomes deeply rooted throughout society, it contributes to the resilience and stability of the country’s financial system. For a developing economy such as Sri Lanka, strengthening domestic savings is particularly important in supporting sustainable economic development.

Having experienced significant economic challenges in recent years, our country must place renewed emphasis on financial discipline, responsible consumption, prudent financial management and long-term planning. However, thrift should never be misunderstood as the complete restriction of consumption or the denial of essential needs.

Rather, it is the ability to identify priorities, distinguish between needs and wants, and utilise available resources intelligently and productively. Living within one’s means, managing unnecessary expenditure, maintaining responsible borrowing practices and systematically saving for future requirements are essential elements of financial thrift. The same principles are equally applicable to the way we utilise our natural resources.

By consuming responsibly, minimising waste and encouraging the reuse of resources, we can generate benefits not only for individual households but also for the wider national economy.

Protecting the environment is also an investment for tomorrow

Climate change, rising global temperatures, water scarcity, deforestation, environmental pollution and the loss of biodiversity are among the most pressing challenges faced by humanity today. These challenges cannot be separated from economic development. Changes in environmental conditions directly affect agriculture, food security, public health, infrastructure, energy requirements and overall economic productivity.

The United Nations’ 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development recognises that economic progress, social wellbeing and environmental protection are interconnected dimensions of sustainable development. In particular, the Sustainable Development Goals relating to clean water and sanitation, affordable and clean energy, sustainable cities and communities, responsible consumption and production, and climate action are closely aligned with the message we seek to communicate through this year’s Thrift Month. One of the most important principles we must recognise is that environmental protection is not the responsibility of governments and environmental organisations alone.

Every citizen has a meaningful role to play

Switching off unnecessary lights, preventing the wastage of water, reducing food waste, limiting the use of single-use plastics, segregating household waste, encouraging recycling and planting and nurturing trees are simple but effective actions through which individuals can contribute towards environmental sustainability.

Energy conservation deserves particular attention. Reducing unnecessary energy consumption can help households manage expenditure while contributing towards the efficient utilisation of national energy resources. Similarly, promoting renewable energy and improving energy efficiency are important steps towards building a more sustainable and resilient economy.

Every drop of water we conserve today, every unit of electricity we save and every tree we plant and nurture represent valuable contributions towards the wellbeing of future generations. Just as we save money in a bank account for our children, we must also preserve a healthy environment and sustainable natural resources for them to inherit. This is the broader philosophy of thrift that the National Savings Bank seeks to promote.

A new banking vision built on environmental and social responsibility

The role of banks and financial institutions is undergoing a significant transformation across the world. Today, the success of a financial institution is increasingly assessed not only through profitability, asset growth and market value, but also through its contribution towards society, environmental sustainability and responsible economic development.

Against this background, the principles of Environmental, Social and Governance responsibility, commonly referred to as ESG, have become an important consideration in modern banking. Environmental responsibility focuses on conserving natural resources, improving energy efficiency and supporting environmentally responsible practices.

Social responsibility encompasses financial inclusion, education, community development, customer protection and the wellbeing of society. Governance responsibility emphasises transparency, accountability, ethical conduct, regulatory compliance and responsible decision-making. As a national financial institution, the responsibility of the National Savings Bank extends beyond accepting deposits and providing banking services.

Having earned the trust of generations of Sri Lankans, we recognise our obligation to contribute towards the long-term development of the country, the wellbeing of society and the preservation of the environment. Strengthening financial literacy, promoting secure savings, expanding access to banking services through technology and ensuring that financial services reach every segment of society remain central to our national mission. Our initiative, themed, “Saving a Tomorrow” represents an effort to translate these broader responsibilities into practical actions that can become part of the everyday lives of our people.

We believe that responsible banking must create value not only for the present generation but also for those who will inherit the future.

NSB SavingsFest 2026: Transforming the philosophy of thrift into national action

The National Savings Bank has traditionally observed October as Thrift Month, culminating in the celebration of World Thrift Day on 31 October. This year, we have sought to give the occasion a broader national significance through NSB SavingsFest 2026, organised under the theme “Saving a Tomorrow.”

What makes this year’s initiative particularly meaningful is our decision to move beyond conventional awareness campaigns and translate the philosophy of thrift into a series of practical, community-oriented activities. The program focuses on environmentally friendly transportation, tree planting, the conservation of water and natural resources, responsible waste management, recycling, the improvement of public spaces and the protection of our national heritage.

Through the message “A Ride to Save Our Trees, A Ride to Preserve Our Waterways, A Ride to Save Tomorrow,” we intend to encourage communities to recognise that the preservation of our environment is an essential part of building a sustainable future. The main celebrations in Colombo will commence at 7.30 a.m. on Saturday, 31 October 2026, with a special cycling parade ceremonially flagged off by the Chairman of the National Savings Bank, Dr. Harsha Cabral, President’s Counsel.

Cycling has been selected as a symbolic element of this year’s program because it brings together several important principles: environmentally responsible transportation, healthier lifestyles and the efficient utilisation of resources. Promoting cycling as an alternative mode of transport, where practical and appropriate, can contribute towards reducing fuel consumption and encouraging more sustainable mobility.

Following the cycling parade, a special tree-planting program is scheduled to take place at 9.30 a.m. in the vicinity of the Gangaramaya Temple in Colombo. The initiative is intended to highlight the importance of urban greenery and the preservation of green spaces for future generations. Tree planting in urban environments is not merely an exercise in beautification. When appropriate species are selected and properly maintained, trees can provide shade, support biodiversity and contribute towards healthier urban surroundings.

The main NSB SavingsFest 2026 Thrift Carnival will commence at 10.30 a.m. at Viharamahadevi Park, Colombo. The carnival is designed to bring together financial awareness, environmental responsibility, local entrepreneurship and community participation within a single public platform. Trade exhibitions, stalls, environmentally friendly activities and awareness programs will provide opportunities for visitors to experience the broader meaning of thrift in a practical and engaging manner.

Emphasis will be placed on reducing unnecessary plastic consumption, promoting recycling and encouraging environmentally responsible lifestyles. We also consider the participation of children and young people especially important. By introducing the principles of thrift, financial responsibility and environmental conservation at an early age, we can help nurture a generation that is better prepared to make responsible decisions about its future.

A national environmental mission extending beyond Colombo

One of the most distinctive features of NSB SavingsFest 2026 is its islandwide character. We have deliberately extended the program beyond Colombo because environmental and social responsibility cannot be confined to a single city or region. Different parts of Sri Lanka face different environmental challenges.

Coastal communities must address issues relating to marine pollution and coastal conservation, while communities in the central highlands face challenges associated with soil erosion, the protection of water catchment areas and landslide risks. Urban communities, meanwhile, must place greater emphasis on waste management, the maintenance of public spaces and the preservation of urban greenery. Recognising these diverse needs, the National Savings Bank has organised a series of regional activities through its extensive branch and regional office network.

In the Northern Province, a cycling parade will be organised in Chunnakam, together with a tree-planting initiative along the Thalsevana coastal area in Kankesanthurai. The program is intended to promote awareness of coastal conservation and the importance of protecting vulnerable coastal ecosystems.

In the Eastern Province, cycling parades, tree-planting programs and SavingsFest activities have been planned in Batticaloa and Uhana. These initiatives seek to encourage community participation, environmentally responsible transportation and the development of greener surroundings.

In the Central Province, a cycling parade and SavingsFest carnival will be organised in Kandy to communicate the message of responsible living and environmental sustainability.

In the Northwestern Province, activities in Kurunegala will include a cycling parade and a program to improve the appearance of the Kurunegala Railway Station. This initiative carries an important message: protecting and maintaining public property is also an essential element of thrift. Public infrastructure belongs to the nation, and its proper maintenance represents responsible stewardship of national resources.

In the Southern Province, programs in Dondra and Matara will focus on recycling, responsible plastic waste management and the protection of the marine environment. Special activities have also been planned in Galle, including the cleaning and preservation of the historic Galle Fort, tree planting and SavingsFest celebrations. These initiatives reinforce the understanding that thrift is not limited to financial resources or the natural environment.

Our historical and cultural heritage is equally valuable and must be preserved for future generations.

In the Sabaragamuwa Province, environmental cleaning, tree planting and urban beautification programs will be carried out in Kegalle and Ratnapura.

In the Uva Province, activities in Badulla will focus on environmental conservation, soil erosion and community awareness of landslide risks. The common objective of these regional programs is to translate the philosophy of thrift into meaningful action according to the specific needs of each community.

From the conservation of coastal environments in the North to the preservation of historical heritage in the South, and from the protection of highland ecosystems to the improvement of urban green spaces, we are working towards one common national objective: safeguarding the future of our country.

We regard this initiative not merely as a promotional campaign conducted by a bank, but as a national message of responsibility carried to the people through a trusted financial institution.

October: A month that connects generations

The Month of October holds particular significance for the National Savings Bank. The World Children’s Day and the International Day of Older Persons are observed on 1 October, followed by the World Teachers’ Day on 5 October, World Post Day on 9 October and World Thrift Day on 31 October. Each of these occasions is closely connected with the national mission of the bank.

Children represent the future of our nation

Developing financial discipline, responsible habits and an understanding of the importance of savings from an early age is an investment in the long-term wellbeing of society. To mark the World Children’s Day this year, the National Savings Bank organised the “Paata Paata Hapankam” Children’s Art Competition under the theme “Big Dreams Through Little Savings.” The program provided an opportunity to recognise the children’s creativity while introducing the importance of saving for their future.

Encouraging a child to dream, appreciating their creativity and building confidence in their abilities are valuable contributions towards their development. At the same time, the knowledge, experience and wisdom of older generations must be recognised and passed on to younger members of society. Meanwhile, the older generations have played a significant role in preserving the traditional values of thrift, financial discipline and responsible living.

World Teachers’ Day also holds a special place in our institutional calendar. This year, through our islandwide network, we had the privilege of visiting schools and personally recognising the teachers for their invaluable contribution towards shaping the future of our children. Teachers play a fundamental role in developing knowledge, discipline, responsibility and positive attitudes among young people. Their contribution towards establishing a culture of thrift and responsible citizenship deserves our highest appreciation.

World Post Day is equally meaningful to the National Savings Bank. The longstanding relationship between the Bank and the Sri Lanka Postal Department represents an important chapter in the history of savings mobilisation in our country. Through the postal network, banking and savings facilities have been brought closer to communities across Sri Lanka, particularly those in rural and underserved areas. This partnership continues to demonstrate the importance of financial inclusion and equitable access to financial services.

Together, these commemorations reflect a common national objective: strengthening the culture of thrift across generations, from children to senior citizens.

Fifty-four years of national service: From a proud heritage to the future of banking

The history of the National Savings Bank is closely intertwined with the development of Sri Lanka’s savings culture. Building upon a savings heritage dating back to 1832, the National Savings Bank was established in 1972 and marks its 54th anniversary in 2026. Throughout this journey, our fundamental responsibility has remained unchanged: encouraging the people of Sri Lanka to save and strengthening their long-term financial security. The National Savings Bank occupies a unique position in the country’s financial sector, with a 100% Government guarantee on deposits and the interest payable on them. This assurance has contributed significantly towards establishing the Bank as a trusted national financial institution.

We regard the confidence placed in us by generations of Sri Lankans not merely as an institutional achievement, but as a responsibility that must be protected and strengthened.

Today, the National Savings Bank serves the country through a network of 263 branches, supported by extensive postal banking facilities. At the same time, we continue to develop modern digital banking solutions, convenient payment facilities and technology-driven services to meet the evolving financial requirements of our customers. Having secured a position among Sri Lanka’s five most valuable brands, the National Savings Bank continues to strengthen its institutional reputation and brand value.

However, our vision for the future extends beyond maintaining our traditional position as a savings institution. While preserving the fundamental values of security, trust and financial discipline, we aspire to become an increasingly modern, digitally enabled, customer-centric and future-oriented bank.

Digital banking provides opportunities for customers to save time, reduce unnecessary travel and conduct financial transactions more conveniently. It also creates opportunities to improve operational efficiency, reduce paper consumption and encourage more responsible resource utilisation.

Therefore, technological advancement and environmental sustainability should not be viewed as competing priorities. Rather, they are complementary dimensions of the future of responsible banking. We believe that the strength of a national financial institution must be measured not only by its financial performance but also by its ability to respond meaningfully to the changing needs of society.

Transforming thrift from a habit into a national culture

The message we seek to communicate during Thrift Month 2026 should not end with the celebrations on 31 October.

It must become a continuing philosophy that begins within the home, extends to schools and workplaces, reaches communities and ultimately becomes deeply rooted throughout the nation. As families, we must save a portion of our income for future needs while also using water, electricity and other household resources responsibly. As schools, we must develop financial literacy among children while nurturing respect for nature, responsible waste management and environmental awareness.

As institutions, we must pursue financial performance while maintaining a strong commitment to resource efficiency, ethical conduct and social responsibility. As a nation, we must pursue economic development while ensuring that our natural resources and national heritage remain available for future generations. This transformation does not necessarily begin with large investments or complex national programs. It begins with small changes in individual attitudes and behaviour.

The decision to avoid an unnecessary expense, the habit of conserving water, the commitment to keeping a public place clean and the willingness of a community to plant and nurture trees are all contributions towards the same national objective. One of the most important truths we must recognise is that the future is not simply something we inherit; it is something we create through the decisions we make today. A sustainable future cannot be achieved through policies and programs alone.

It requires a collective commitment to responsible behaviour, thoughtful consumption and respect for the resources upon which our lives depend.

Our responsibility towards the generations yet to come

Every generation aspires to leave behind a better future for its children. However, fulfilling that aspiration requires more than accumulating financial wealth, property and material assets. Our children deserve to inherit clean air, safe water, fertile land, healthy ecosystems, rich biodiversity and a proud national heritage. They must also inherit the values of financial discipline, responsible consumption, social cooperation and respect for the environment.

As the National Savings Bank, our ambition is to strengthen this broader understanding of thrift throughout Sri Lankan society. Our institutional heritage, financial strength, nationwide service network and the confidence placed in us by the people provide a strong foundation for advancing this national mission.

Nevertheless, this is not a responsibility that the National Savings Bank can fulfil alone. It requires the active participation of public and private institutions, schools, universities, environmental organisations, local communities, entrepreneurs, young people and the wider public.

Therefore, I extend a warm and sincere invitation to all Sri Lankans to join us at NSB SavingsFest 2026, taking place at Viharamahadevi Park in Colombo and at selected locations across the country on 31 October 2026. On this occasion, we will come together not merely to commemorate World Thrift Day, but to promote a renewed national understanding of thrift and its relevance to the future of our country.

Every Rupee we save today contributes towards financial security tomorrow. Every drop of water we conserve today is a valuable resource preserved for future generations. Every unit of energy we save contributes towards the responsible management of our national resources. Every tree we plant, and nurture today may provide shade and environmental benefits for generations to come. Similarly, every element of our national heritage that we protect today helps preserve the identity, history and dignity of our nation.

Saving for the future is not merely about setting aside a portion of what we possess today. It is about ensuring that the resources we enjoy in the present remain available for those who will come after us.

The success of our generation should not be measured solely by the wealth we accumulate or the resources we consume, but by the value of the resources, opportunities and heritage we preserve for future generations. As the National Savings Bank marks 54 years of national service, we are committed to giving renewed meaning to our longstanding mission by transforming thrift from a financial habit into a national philosophy of responsible living.

Because what we must save today is not merely money, but tomorrow itself.

Together with National Savings Bank – Let us ‘Save a Tomorrow!’
